title: Ch 4 · Exploring Diversity of Matter using Separation Techniques

questions.q: Separating mixtures into their constituents helps us to
choices: change the boiling point of water
questions.explain: Separating mixtures lets useful constituents be recovered and used again. This helps to reduce waste and to reuse and recycle resources.
questions.lo: State why separation techniques are needed for sustainable living

notes.0: Separating a mixture does not change the boiling point of water. Think about what can be done with the useful parts once they are separated.
notes.1: Separating mixtures lets useful parts be recovered, so it lowers waste rather than adding to it. Think about what happens to the recovered parts.
notes.2: Separation is a physical process, so no new elements are made. Think about what can be done with the useful parts once they are separated.

why.right: Separating mixtures supports sustainable living because useful constituents can be recovered and used again instead of thrown away.
wrong: Separating mixtures supports sustainable living because each separation turns waste into brand new elements.
Separating mixtures supports sustainable living because separated substances never need to be replaced or bought again.

questions.q: Water that is safe for drinking is called
questions.explain: Potable water is water that is safe to drink. Tap water in Singapore is treated so that it is potable.
questions.lo: State why separation techniques are needed for sustainable living

notes.0: Groundwater is water found under the ground. It must be treated before it is safe to drink. Think about the term for drinkable water.
notes.2: Used water comes from homes and industries, and it is not safe to drink until it is treated. Think about the term for drinkable water.
notes.3: Seawater contains too much salt to drink. Think about the term for water that is safe to drink.

questions.q: Separation is possible because constituents of a mixture
questions.explain: The constituents of a mixture are not chemically combined, so each keeps its own physical properties. Differences in these properties let them be separated.
questions.lo: State the properties and factors used to choose a separation technique

notes.0: If the constituents had the same boiling point, distillation could not separate them. Separation uses a difference between the constituents.
notes.1: A mixture does not form a new substance. Think about what each constituent still has after it is mixed in.
notes.3: Chemically combined constituents form a compound, which is hard to separate. Think about how constituents in a mixture are held together.

why.right: Mixtures can be separated because each constituent keeps physical properties, such as boiling point, that differ from the others.
wrong: Mixtures can be separated because their constituents react with each other to form a new substance.
Mixtures can be separated because all of their constituents have exactly the same physical properties.

questions.q: Besides physical properties, which factor affects the choice of technique?
questions.explain: Besides physical properties, cost affects the choice of separation technique. A technique that uses a lot of energy or expensive equipment may cost too much.
questions.lo: State the properties and factors used to choose a separation technique

notes.1: The name of a mixture does not change how it can be separated. Think about how much a technique needs in energy and equipment.
notes.2: These techniques all work at normal room temperature, so the room temperature does not decide which one is chosen. Think about how much a technique needs in energy and equipment.
notes.3: The same mixture can be separated in beakers of any shape. Think about how much a technique needs in energy and equipment.

why.right: Cost affects the choice of technique because some techniques need a lot of energy or expensive equipment.
wrong: Cost affects the choice of technique because the most expensive technique always gives the purest product.
Cost affects the choice of technique because cheaper techniques always separate mixtures more quickly.

questions.q: Why is reverse osmosis not the only method used for potable water in Singapore?
questions.explain: Reverse osmosis needs a lot of energy to push water through the membrane, so it is costly. Singapore also uses other sources to keep costs down.
questions.lo: State the properties and factors used to choose a separation technique

notes.0: Reverse osmosis does need electricity to push water through the membrane at high pressure. Think about what using a lot of electricity means.
notes.1: Reverse osmosis produces water that is safe to drink. Think about what it needs to run and what that means.
notes.3: Reverse osmosis does remove salt from seawater. Think about what it needs to run and what that means.

why.right: Reverse osmosis is not the only method because pushing water through its membrane uses a lot of energy.
wrong: Reverse osmosis is not the only method because its membrane lets salt particles pass through.
Reverse osmosis is not the only method because it adds harmful bacteria back into the water.

questions.q: Magnetic attraction separates substances based on whether they are
questions.explain: Magnetic attraction separates substances that are attracted to a magnet, such as iron, from those that are not.
questions.lo: Separate magnetic from non-magnetic substances using magnetic attraction

notes.0: Solubility in water is used in filtration and evaporation, not magnetic attraction. Think about what a magnet does to some materials.
notes.1: Particle size is used in filtration. Think about what a magnet does to some materials.
notes.2: Boiling points are used in distillation. Think about what a magnet does to some materials.

questions.q: A magnet is placed near iron filings and sulfur. What is left behind?
questions.explain: Iron is attracted to the magnet, but sulfur is not. So the iron filings are removed and the sulfur is left behind.
questions.lo: Separate magnetic from non-magnetic substances using magnetic attraction

notes.0: Iron filings are magnetic, so the magnet pulls them out of the mixture. Think about which substance the magnet does not attract.
notes.2: Only one of the two substances is attracted to a magnet. Think about which one stays behind.
notes.3: Iron filings are attracted to the magnet, so they are removed, not left behind.

why.right: Sulfur is left behind because it is not attracted to a magnet, while iron is.
wrong: Sulfur is left behind because it is heavier than iron, so the magnet cannot lift it.
Sulfur is left behind because a magnet attracts only substances that are soluble in water.

questions.q: A magnet passes over scrap metal. Which metal is removed?
questions.explain: Iron is a magnetic material, so it is attracted to the magnet. Aluminium and copper are metals, but they are not magnetic.
questions.lo: Separate magnetic from non-magnetic substances using magnetic attraction

notes.1: Aluminium is a metal, but it is not attracted to a magnet. Not every metal is magnetic.
notes.2: Copper is a metal, but it is not attracted to a magnet. Not every metal is magnetic.

why.right: Iron is removed because it is a magnetic material and is attracted to the magnet.
wrong: Iron is removed because every metal, including aluminium and copper, is attracted to a magnet.
Iron is removed because it is the heaviest metal in the scrap pile.

questions.q: Which object in a scrapyard is picked up by a magnet?
questions.explain: Steel contains iron, so steel bolts are attracted to a magnet. Plastic, rubber and glass are not magnetic.
questions.lo: Separate magnetic from non-magnetic substances using magnetic attraction

notes.0: Plastic is not attracted to a magnet. Think about which object contains iron.
notes.2: Rubber is not attracted to a magnet. Think about which object contains iron.
notes.3: Glass is not attracted to a magnet, even with a shiny coating. Think about which object contains iron.

why.right: Steel bolts are picked up because steel contains iron, which is attracted to a magnet.
wrong: Steel bolts are picked up because they are the smallest and lightest objects in the scrapyard.
Steel bolts are picked up because every hard solid object is attracted to a magnet.

questions.q: Which mixture can be separated using a magnet?
questions.explain: Steel pins contain iron and are attracted to a magnet, but sand is not. So a magnet can pull the pins out of the sand.
questions.lo: Separate magnetic from non-magnetic substances using magnetic attraction

notes.1: Ink and water are not magnetic, so a magnet cannot separate them. Look for a mixture with one magnetic constituent.
notes.2: Copper and aluminium are metals, but neither is magnetic. Look for a mixture with one magnetic constituent.
notes.3: Salt and sand are not magnetic, so a magnet cannot separate them. Look for a mixture with one magnetic constituent.

why.right: Steel pins and sand can be separated by a magnet because only the steel is attracted to it.
wrong: Steel pins and sand can be separated by a magnet because both of them are attracted to it.
Steel pins and sand can be separated by a magnet because sand dissolves when the magnet is near.

questions.q: Filtration separates substances with different
questions.explain: Filtration separates substances by particle size. Small particles pass through the pores of the filter paper, but large particles are trapped.
questions.lo: Describe filtration and identify the residue and filtrate

notes.0: Filtration is used on insoluble solids, but the filter paper itself sorts particles using its tiny holes. Think about what the holes allow through.
notes.1: Magnetic properties are used in magnetic attraction, not filtration. Think about the tiny holes in filter paper.
notes.3: Boiling points are used in distillation, not filtration. Think about the tiny holes in filter paper.

why.right: Filtration separates by particle size because the pores in filter paper let small particles through but trap large ones.
wrong: Filtration separates by particle size because the filter paper heats the mixture and boils off small particles.
Filtration separates by particle size because large particles dissolve in the filter paper and disappear.

questions.q: The solid left on the filter paper is called the
questions.explain: The residue is the solid left on the filter paper after filtration. The liquid that passes through is the filtrate.
questions.lo: Describe filtration and identify the residue and filtrate

notes.0: The filtrate is the liquid that passes through the filter paper. Think about the name for what stays on the paper.
notes.1: The distillate is the liquid collected in distillation. Think about the name for what stays on the filter paper.
notes.2: The solvent is the liquid in which a solute dissolves. Think about the name for the solid that stays on the filter paper.

questions.q: The liquid that passes through the filter paper is called the
questions.explain: The filtrate is the liquid that passes through the filter paper. The solid that stays on the paper is the residue.
questions.lo: Describe filtration and identify the residue and filtrate

notes.0: A solute is a substance that dissolves. Think about the name for the liquid that comes through the filter paper.
notes.2: The residue is the solid that stays on the filter paper. Think about the name for what passes through.
notes.3: The distillate is the liquid collected in distillation. Think about the name for the liquid collected in filtration.

questions.q: Chalk and water are filtered. What is the residue?
questions.explain: Chalk is insoluble in water, so its particles are too large to pass through the filter paper. Chalk is the residue and water is the filtrate.
questions.lo: Describe filtration and identify the residue and filtrate

notes.0: The water passes through the filter paper, so it is not part of what stays behind. Think about which substance is trapped.
notes.1: The filter paper is part of the apparatus, not part of the mixture. Think about which substance from the mixture is trapped on it.
notes.3: Water passes through the filter paper, so it is the filtrate. Think about which substance is trapped on the paper.

why.right: Chalk is the residue because it is insoluble and its particles are too large to pass through the filter paper.
wrong: Chalk is the residue because it dissolves in water and the solution stays on the filter paper.
Chalk is the residue because it is the liquid part of the mixture that passes through.

questions.q: Tea is poured through a tea strainer. What is the filtrate?
questions.explain: The liquid tea passes through the strainer, so it is the filtrate. The tea leaves are too large to pass through, so they are the residue.
questions.lo: Describe filtration and identify the residue and filtrate

notes.1: Tea leaves are too large to pass through the strainer, so they are the residue. Think about what passes through.
notes.2: Only part of the mixture passes through the strainer. Think about which part flows into the cup.
notes.3: The strainer works like filter paper. It is part of the apparatus, not the filtrate. Think about what passes through it.

why.right: The liquid tea is the filtrate because it is the part that passes through the holes of the strainer.
wrong: The liquid tea is the filtrate because it is the part that stays behind in the strainer.
The liquid tea is the filtrate because the strainer changes the leaves into a liquid.

questions.q: Sand and water are filtered. Sand is left on the paper because sand particles are
questions.explain: Sand particles are bigger than the pores of the filter paper, so they cannot pass through. Water particles are small enough to pass through.
questions.lo: Describe filtration and identify the residue and filtrate

notes.0: Sand is not magnetic, and filter paper does not use magnetism. Think about the size of sand particles compared with the holes in the paper.
notes.1: Sand is insoluble in water. A soluble substance would pass through the paper. Think about particle size compared with the holes in the paper.
notes.2: Particles smaller than the pores would pass through the filter paper with the water. Think about why sand stays on top.

why.right: Sand stays on the filter paper because its particles are too large to fit through the pores.
wrong: Sand stays on the filter paper because its particles are attracted to the fibres of the paper.
Sand stays on the filter paper because it dissolves in the water and then sticks to the paper.

questions.q: The residue is sand and the filtrate is water. What was filtered?
questions.explain: Sand is insoluble and stays on the filter paper as the residue. Water passes through as the filtrate. So the mixture was sand and water.
questions.lo: Describe filtration and identify the residue and filtrate

notes.0: Salt dissolves in water and would pass through with it. No salt would be left as a residue. Think about which solid was trapped.
notes.1: Sugar dissolves in water and would pass through with it. Think about which solid was trapped on the paper.
notes.3: Iron and sand are both solids, so no liquid filtrate would come from them. Think about where the water came from.

why.right: The mixture was sand and water because sand is insoluble and stays behind while water passes through.
wrong: The mixture was sand and water because filtration turns part of the water into sand.
The mixture was sand and water because dissolved substances always stay on the filter paper.

questions.q: Why can salt not be separated from salt solution by filtration?
choices: dissolved salt passes through the filter paper
salt particles are bigger than the pores
salt has a low boiling point
questions.explain: Salt dissolves in water, and its dissolved particles are small enough to pass through the filter paper. So filtration cannot trap the salt.
questions.lo: Describe filtration and identify the residue and filtrate

notes.0: Salt is not magnetic, and magnetism has nothing to do with filtration. Think about what happens to salt when it dissolves.
notes.2: If salt particles were bigger than the pores, filtration would trap them. Think about the size of salt particles once they dissolve.
notes.3: Boiling point matters in distillation, not filtration. Think about what happens to salt when it dissolves.

why.right: Dissolved salt cannot be filtered because its particles are small enough to pass through the filter paper pores.
wrong: Dissolved salt cannot be filtered because its particles are too large to reach the filter paper.
Dissolved salt cannot be filtered because salt melts as soon as it touches the filter paper.

questions.q: Evaporation is used to obtain
choices: an insoluble solid from a liquid
a pure liquid from a solution
a dissolved solid from a solution
questions.explain: Evaporation removes the solvent as vapour and leaves the dissolved solid behind. It is used to obtain a dissolved solid from a solution.
questions.lo: Describe evaporation to obtain a dissolved solid from a solution

notes.0: An insoluble solid is separated from a liquid by filtration. Evaporation is used when the solid has dissolved.
notes.1: Iron is removed from a mixture with a magnet. Think about what is left when the solvent of a solution is removed.
notes.2: In evaporation the solvent escapes as vapour and is not collected. Think about what is left behind in the dish.

why.right: Evaporation obtains a dissolved solid because the solvent turns into vapour and leaves the solid behind.
wrong: Evaporation obtains a dissolved solid because the solid turns into vapour and is collected separately.
Evaporation obtains a dissolved solid because heating makes the solid particles too big to dissolve.

questions.q: In evaporation, the solvent is removed because it
choices: changes to a gas at a lower temperature
questions.explain: The solvent changes to a gas at a much lower temperature than the dissolved solid. So heating removes the solvent and leaves the solid behind.
questions.lo: Describe evaporation to obtain a dissolved solid from a solution

notes.1: Particle size is used in filtration, not evaporation. Think about what heating does to the solvent.
notes.2: No filter paper is used in evaporation, so nothing stays on it. Think about what heating does to the solvent.
notes.3: Magnetism is used in magnetic attraction, not evaporation. Think about what heating does to the solvent.

why.right: The solvent is removed in evaporation because it turns into a gas at a lower temperature than the solute.
wrong: The solvent is removed in evaporation because heating makes its particles too large to stay in the dish.
The solvent is removed in evaporation because the solute turns into a gas first and pushes it out.

questions.q: Salt solution is heated until all the water evaporates. What is left?
questions.explain: Water evaporates when the salt solution is heated, but salt does not. So solid salt is left behind in the dish.
questions.lo: Describe evaporation to obtain a dissolved solid from a solution

notes.1: Only the water evaporates. The dissolved salt stays behind. Think about what remains in the dish.
notes.2: All the water has evaporated, so there is no solution left. Think about what remains when the solvent is gone.
notes.3: The water has evaporated, so it has left the dish. Think about what stays behind.

why.right: Salt is left behind because water turns into vapour at a much lower temperature than salt does.
wrong: Salt is left behind because the water reacts with the salt and turns into solid salt.
Salt is left behind because salt particles are too big to dissolve in hot water.

questions.q: Distillation separates substances with different
questions.explain: Distillation separates substances with different boiling points. The substance with the lower boiling point boils first, and its vapour is cooled and collected.
questions.lo: Describe distillation and the role of each part of the set-up

notes.0: Magnetic properties are used in magnetic attraction. Think about what distillation does to the mixture when it is heated.
notes.1: Colours are separated by chromatography. Think about what distillation does to the mixture when it is heated.
notes.2: Particle size is used in filtration. Think about what distillation does to the mixture when it is heated.

why.right: Distillation works because the substance with the lower boiling point turns into vapour first and is collected.
wrong: Distillation works because the substance with the larger particles turns into vapour first and is collected.
Distillation works because every substance in the mixture boils at exactly the same temperature.

questions.q: Distillation involves
questions.explain: In distillation, the liquid is boiled to form vapour. The vapour is then cooled in the condenser and condenses back into a liquid.
questions.lo: Describe distillation and the role of each part of the set-up

notes.0: Melting and freezing change solids and liquids, not liquids and vapour. Think about how vapour is made and then turned back into liquid.
notes.2: Dissolving and filtering are used in other techniques. Think about how vapour is made and then turned back into liquid.
notes.3: Boiling is part of distillation, but the vapour is not frozen. Think about how vapour is turned back into a liquid.

why.right: Distillation uses boiling and condensation because the liquid is turned into vapour and then cooled back into liquid.
wrong: Distillation uses boiling and condensation because the solid is melted first and then frozen again.
Distillation uses boiling and condensation because the vapour is trapped on filter paper as it cools.

questions.q: The pure liquid collected in distillation is called the
questions.explain: The distillate is the pure liquid collected after the vapour condenses in distillation.
questions.lo: Describe distillation and the role of each part of the set-up

notes.0: The residue is the solid left on filter paper in filtration. Think about the name for the liquid collected in distillation.
notes.1: The filtrate is the liquid that passes through filter paper. Think about the name for the liquid collected in distillation.
notes.3: A solute is a substance that dissolves. Think about the name for the liquid collected in distillation.

questions.q: What is the function of the condenser?
choices: to cool the vapour into a liquid
questions.explain: The condenser is cooled by cold running water. It cools the hot vapour so that it condenses into a liquid, which is collected as the distillate.
questions.lo: Describe distillation and the role of each part of the set-up

notes.0: The mixture is heated by the burner under the flask. Think about what happens to the vapour as it passes through the condenser.
notes.1: The flask is held steady by a clamp. Think about what happens to the vapour as it passes through the condenser.
notes.3: The boiling point is read with the thermometer. Think about what happens to the vapour as it passes through the condenser.

why.right: The condenser turns vapour into liquid because cold water around it takes heat away from the vapour.
wrong: The condenser turns vapour into liquid because it heats the vapour until it melts.
The condenser turns vapour into liquid because it has pores that trap the vapour particles.

questions.q: What is the function of boiling chips?
questions.explain: Boiling chips help bubbles form evenly as the liquid boils. This makes boiling smoother and stops the liquid from boiling up suddenly and violently.
questions.lo: Describe distillation and the role of each part of the set-up

notes.1: The vapour is cooled by the condenser. Think about what happens to the boiling liquid in the flask.
notes.2: Boiling chips do not absorb salt. Think about how the liquid boils in the flask with and without them.
notes.3: Boiling chips do not change the boiling point of the liquid. Think about how the liquid boils with and without them.

why.right: Boiling chips smooth the boiling because small bubbles form evenly on their rough surfaces.
wrong: Boiling chips smooth the boiling because they lower the boiling point of the liquid.
Boiling chips smooth the boiling because they absorb the dissolved salt from the liquid.

questions.q: Salt solution is distilled. What remains in the distillation flask?
questions.explain: Water boils off, condenses and is collected as the distillate. Salt has a much higher boiling point, so it stays in the distillation flask.
questions.lo: Describe distillation and the role of each part of the set-up

notes.0: Pure water is collected in the receiver as the distillate, not left in the flask. Think about what cannot boil off.
notes.1: Only the water boils off. Think about the substance with the much higher boiling point.
notes.2: Steam leaves the flask and goes into the condenser. Think about the substance that does not boil off.

why.right: Salt stays in the distillation flask because its boiling point is far higher than that of water.
wrong: Salt stays in the distillation flask because its particles are too big to pass through the condenser.
Salt stays in the distillation flask because it is attracted to the glass of the flask.

questions.q: In a distillation, which substance in the mixture turns into vapour first?
choices: the one with the largest particles
the one with the lowest boiling point
the one with the highest boiling point
questions.explain: The substance with the lowest boiling point reaches its boiling point first as the mixture is heated. So it turns into vapour first.
questions.lo: Describe distillation and the role of each part of the set-up

notes.0: Particle size matters in filtration, not in boiling. Think about which substance reaches its boiling point first as the temperature rises.
notes.2: Magnetism has nothing to do with boiling. Think about which substance reaches its boiling point first as the temperature rises.
notes.3: A substance with a high boiling point needs a higher temperature before it boils. Think about which boils first as the temperature rises.

why.right: The substance with the lowest boiling point boils first because it needs the lowest temperature to boil.
wrong: The substance with the lowest boiling point boils first because it has the largest particles.
The substance with the lowest boiling point boils first because it is the heaviest substance.

questions.q: The cold water supply to the condenser is turned off. What happens?
questions.explain: Without cold water, the condenser cannot cool the vapour well. Much of the vapour escapes without condensing, so less distillate is collected.
questions.lo: Describe distillation and the role of each part of the set-up

notes.0: Cold water is needed to cool the vapour into liquid. Think about what happens to the vapour when the condenser is no longer cooled.
notes.1: The flask is still heated by the burner. Think about what happens to the vapour when the condenser is no longer cooled.
notes.2: The water supply cools the condenser, not the flask, so the salt stays where it is. Think about what happens to the vapour.

why.right: Less distillate is collected because a warm condenser cannot cool all of the vapour into liquid.
wrong: Less distillate is collected because the cold water was what made the mixture boil.
Less distillate is collected because the vapour freezes inside a condenser with no water.

questions.q: Paper chromatography separates substances that
choices: dissolve to different extents in a solvent
questions.explain: In paper chromatography, substances dissolve in the solvent to different extents. More soluble substances travel further up the paper, so they separate.
questions.lo: Interpret a paper chromatogram

notes.0: Boiling points are used in distillation. Think about what the solvent does as it moves up the paper.
notes.1: Magnetic properties are used in magnetic attraction. Think about what the solvent does as it moves up the paper.
notes.3: Particle size is used in filtration. Think about what the solvent does as it moves up the paper.

why.right: Chromatography separates substances because more soluble substances are carried further up the paper by the solvent.
wrong: Chromatography separates substances because substances with lower boiling points evaporate further up the paper.
Chromatography separates substances because larger particles are trapped by the pores at the start line.

questions.q: The paper with separated coloured spots is called a
questions.explain: A chromatogram is the paper with separated spots produced by paper chromatography.
questions.lo: Interpret a paper chromatogram

notes.0: The filtrate is the liquid from filtration. Think about the name for the paper produced in chromatography.
notes.2: The distillate is the liquid collected in distillation. Think about the name for the paper produced in chromatography.
notes.3: The residue is the solid left on filter paper. Think about the name for the paper produced in chromatography.

questions.q: On a chromatogram, the spot that travels furthest is the
questions.explain: The most soluble substance dissolves the most in the solvent. So it is carried furthest up the paper.
questions.lo: Interpret a paper chromatogram

notes.1: A less soluble substance is carried only a short way up the paper. Think about which substance the solvent carries the furthest.
notes.2: An insoluble substance does not move at all and stays on the start line. Think about which substance the solvent carries the furthest.
notes.3: Chromatography separates by solubility in the solvent, not by mass. Think about which substance the solvent carries the furthest.

why.right: The spot that travels furthest is the most soluble because it dissolves the most in the moving solvent.
wrong: The spot that travels furthest is the most soluble because it has the highest boiling point.
The spot that travels furthest is the most soluble because it is the lightest coloured substance.

questions.q: A spot remains on the start line. This substance is
questions.explain: An insoluble substance does not dissolve in the solvent. So the solvent cannot carry it, and it stays on the start line.
questions.lo: Interpret a paper chromatogram

notes.1: A very soluble substance is carried far up the paper. Think about why a substance would not move at all.
notes.2: The solvent moves up the paper and does not form a spot. Think about why a substance would not move at all.
notes.3: Magnetism has nothing to do with chromatography. Think about why a substance would not move at all.

why.right: A spot stays on the start line because the substance does not dissolve in the solvent.
wrong: A spot stays on the start line because the substance dissolves fully and stays where it was put.
A spot stays on the start line because the substance has a very low boiling point.

questions.q: An ink gives three separate spots. How many coloured substances does it contain?
questions.explain: Each spot on a chromatogram is a different substance. Three separate spots mean the ink contains three coloured substances.
questions.lo: Interpret a paper chromatogram

notes.0: A single substance gives only one spot. Count the number of separate spots.
notes.2: Each separate spot is a different substance. Count the spots again.
notes.3: Each spot shows one substance, so the count matches the number of spots. Count the spots again.

why.right: The number of spots shows the number of coloured substances because each substance travels its own distance.
wrong: The number of spots shows the number of coloured substances because each substance splits into two spots.
The number of spots shows the number of coloured substances because each spot is a different solvent.

questions.q: Spots move 2 cm, 5 cm and 7 cm. Which belongs to the least soluble substance?
questions.explain: The least soluble substance is carried the shortest distance by the solvent. So the spot at 2 cm belongs to the least soluble substance.
questions.lo: Interpret a paper chromatogram

notes.0: The spot at 7 cm travelled furthest, so it is the most soluble. Think about how far a less soluble substance is carried.
notes.1: The spot at 5 cm is in the middle. Think about how far the least soluble substance is carried.

why.right: The least soluble substance travels the shortest distance because it dissolves less in the moving solvent.
wrong: The least soluble substance travels the shortest distance because it has the lowest boiling point.
The least soluble substance travels the shortest distance because it is the darkest colour on the paper.

questions.q: Dye P gives one spot at 4 cm. Ink Q gives spots at 4 cm and 6 cm. Which is correct?
questions.explain: Ink Q has a spot at 4 cm, the same height as dye P. So Q contains P, along with another substance at 6 cm.
questions.lo: Interpret a paper chromatogram

notes.0: Ink Q gives two spots, so it contains two substances. A pure substance gives only one spot.
notes.1: Dye P gives only one spot, so it cannot contain all of Q. Compare which spots appear in each chromatogram.
notes.2: P gives one spot and Q gives two, so they are not the same. Compare which spots appear in each chromatogram.

why.right: Ink Q contains dye P because one spot of Q travelled the same distance as the spot of P.
wrong: Ink Q contains dye P because Q has more spots, so it must contain every other dye.
Ink Q contains dye P because both spots of Q travelled further than the spot of P.

questions.q: Which technique obtains water from muddy water?
questions.explain: Mud is insoluble in water, so it can be trapped by filter paper. Filtration obtains water from muddy water as the filtrate.
questions.lo: Choose a suitable separation technique for a given mixture

notes.1: Chromatography separates dissolved coloured substances. Mud is insoluble. Think about a method that traps insoluble solids.
notes.2: Mud and water are not magnetic. Think about a method that traps insoluble solids.
notes.3: Evaporation removes the water as vapour, so the water would be lost. Think about a method that keeps the water and traps the mud.

why.right: Filtration obtains water from muddy water because the mud particles are too large to pass through the filter paper.
wrong: Filtration obtains water from muddy water because the mud dissolves and is trapped by the filter paper.
Filtration obtains water from muddy water because the filter paper boils away the mud.

questions.q: Which technique obtains pure water from sugar solution?
questions.explain: Distillation boils the water off and condenses it as pure water. The sugar does not boil off, so it stays in the flask.
questions.lo: Choose a suitable separation technique for a given mixture

notes.0: Sugar and water are not magnetic. Think about a method that collects the water after it boils.
notes.1: Evaporation lets the water escape as vapour, so the water is lost. Think about a method that collects the water.
notes.3: Dissolved sugar passes through filter paper with the water. Think about a method that collects the water after it boils.

why.right: Distillation obtains pure water from sugar solution because the water boils off and is condensed and collected.
wrong: Distillation obtains pure water from sugar solution because the sugar boils off first and leaves the water.
Distillation obtains pure water from sugar solution because the condenser filters out the dissolved sugar.

questions.q: Which technique obtains iron filings from sand?
questions.explain: Iron filings are attracted to a magnet, but sand is not. So a magnet can pull the iron filings out of the sand.
questions.lo: Choose a suitable separation technique for a given mixture

notes.0: Distillation is used for liquids with different boiling points. Iron and sand are dry solids. Think about a property only iron has.
notes.2: Iron filings and sand are both insoluble solids, so filtration cannot separate them. Think about a property only iron has.
notes.3: Evaporation removes a liquid, and there is no liquid here. Think about a property only iron has.

why.right: A magnet separates iron filings from sand because only the iron is attracted to the magnet.
wrong: A magnet separates iron filings from sand because the sand is attracted while the iron is not.
A magnet separates iron filings from sand because the magnet dissolves the sand.

questions.q: Which technique obtains solid salt from salt solution?
questions.explain: Evaporation removes the water as vapour and leaves the dissolved salt behind as a solid.
questions.lo: Choose a suitable separation technique for a given mixture

notes.0: Dissolved salt passes through filter paper with the water. Think about how to remove the water and keep the salt.
notes.1: Salt is not magnetic. Think about how to remove the water and keep the salt.
notes.2: Chromatography separates coloured substances in small amounts. Think about how to remove the water and keep the salt.

why.right: Evaporation obtains solid salt because heating turns the water into vapour and leaves the salt behind.
wrong: Evaporation obtains solid salt because heating makes the salt particles too big to stay dissolved.
Evaporation obtains solid salt because heating turns the salt into vapour, which is then collected.

questions.q: Which technique separates the dyes in a food colouring?
questions.explain: The dyes in food colouring dissolve in the solvent to different extents. Chromatography separates them into separate spots on the paper.
questions.lo: Choose a suitable separation technique for a given mixture

notes.1: The dyes are dissolved, so they pass through filter paper together. Think about a method that separates dissolved coloured substances.
notes.2: Evaporation would leave all the dyes behind together. Think about a method that separates dissolved coloured substances.
notes.3: Dyes are not magnetic. Think about a method that separates dissolved coloured substances.

why.right: Chromatography separates the dyes because each dye dissolves in the solvent to a different extent.
wrong: Chromatography separates the dyes because each dye has a different particle size trapped by the paper.
Chromatography separates the dyes because each dye boils off the paper at a different temperature.

questions.q: A student wants solid sugar from sugar solution. Which technique?
questions.explain: Evaporation removes the water as vapour and leaves the dissolved sugar behind as a solid.
questions.lo: Choose a suitable separation technique for a given mixture

notes.0: Dissolved sugar passes through filter paper with the water. Think about how to remove the water and keep the sugar.
notes.1: Chromatography separates coloured substances in small amounts. Think about how to remove the water and keep the sugar.
notes.2: Sugar is not magnetic. Think about how to remove the water and keep the sugar.

why.right: Evaporation obtains solid sugar because the water turns into vapour and leaves the sugar behind.
wrong: Evaporation obtains solid sugar because the sugar turns into vapour and is collected as a solid.
Evaporation obtains solid sugar because heating makes the sugar insoluble so it is trapped on filter paper.

questions.q: Pure water was obtained and solid salt was left behind. Which technique was used?
questions.explain: Distillation collects the water as pure distillate after it boils and condenses. The salt does not boil off, so it is left behind in the flask.
questions.lo: Choose a suitable separation technique for a given mixture

notes.0: Salt and water are not magnetic. Think about a method that collects the water and leaves the salt behind.
notes.1: Dissolved salt passes through filter paper, so filtration would not leave salt behind. Think about a method that boils the water off.
notes.3: Chromatography separates coloured substances on paper. Think about a method that collects the water and leaves the salt behind.

why.right: Distillation gives both products because the water boils off and is condensed, while the salt stays behind.
wrong: Distillation gives both products because the salt boils off first and is condensed, while water stays.
Distillation gives both products because the condenser filters the salt out of the water.

questions.q: Iron filings, salt and sawdust are mixed. What is done first?
questions.explain: Iron filings are attracted to a magnet, so they can be removed first while the mixture is dry. Salt and sawdust are then separated by other steps.
questions.lo: Order techniques to separate a mixture of three constituents

notes.0: The mixture is dry, so there is no liquid to evaporate. Think about which constituent can be removed easily from the dry mixture.
notes.2: Distillation is used for liquids, and this mixture is dry solids. Think about which constituent can be removed easily from the dry mixture.
notes.3: Filtering a dry mixture does nothing, since all of it stays on the paper. Think about which constituent can be removed easily from the dry mixture.

why.right: Using a magnet comes first because the iron filings can be pulled out easily while the mixture is dry.
wrong: Using a magnet comes first because a magnet attracts the salt and the sawdust as well as the iron.
Using a magnet comes first because the magnet dissolves the salt so it can be filtered.

questions.q: After removing iron, salt and sawdust are stirred in water. Sawdust is removed by
questions.explain: Salt dissolves in water but sawdust does not. Filtration traps the sawdust on the filter paper, and the salt solution passes through.
questions.lo: Order techniques to separate a mixture of three constituents

notes.0: The iron has already been removed, and sawdust is not magnetic. Think about a method that traps insoluble solids.
notes.2: Evaporation would leave the sawdust and the salt behind together. Think about a method that traps insoluble solids.
notes.3: Distillation collects the water and leaves the sawdust and salt behind together. Think about a method that traps insoluble solids.

why.right: Sawdust is removed by filtration because it is insoluble and its pieces are too large to pass through the filter paper.
wrong: Sawdust is removed by filtration because it dissolves in water and the solution stays on the paper.
Sawdust is removed by filtration because it has a lower boiling point than the water.

questions.q: Salt solution is left after removing the sawdust. Solid salt is obtained by
questions.explain: Evaporation removes the water as vapour and leaves the salt behind as a solid.
questions.lo: Order techniques to separate a mixture of three constituents

notes.0: Chromatography separates coloured substances on paper. Think about how to remove the water and keep the salt.
notes.1: Salt is not magnetic. Think about how to remove the water and keep the salt.
notes.3: Dissolved salt passes through filter paper with the water. Think about how to remove the water and keep the salt.

why.right: Solid salt is obtained by evaporation because heating turns the water into vapour and leaves the salt behind.
wrong: Solid salt is obtained by evaporation because heating turns the salt into vapour and leaves the water.
Solid salt is obtained by evaporation because heating makes the salt too large to pass through filter paper.

questions.q: To get pure water from muddy salt water, which order is correct?
questions.explain: Filtration first removes the insoluble mud. Distillation then boils off the water and condenses it as pure water, leaving the salt behind.
questions.lo: Order techniques to separate a mixture of three constituents

notes.0: Evaporation lets the water escape as vapour, so no pure water would be collected. Think about a method that collects the water after it boils.
notes.1: Evaporating first would lose the water as vapour. Think about a method that collects the water after it boils.
notes.2: Chromatography separates coloured substances on paper and does not collect water. Think about a method that collects the water after it boils.

why.right: Filtration then distillation works because filtration removes the mud and distillation collects pure water from the salt solution.
wrong: Filtration then distillation works because filtration removes the salt and distillation removes the mud.
Filtration then distillation works because distillation must always come after any other technique.

questions.q: Sand and salt are mixed. Which order gives dry salt?
questions.explain: Adding water dissolves the salt but not the sand. Filtering removes the sand, and evaporating the filtrate leaves dry salt.
questions.lo: Order techniques to separate a mixture of three constituents

notes.1: Evaporating before filtering would leave the sand and salt mixed together again. Think about when the sand must be removed.
notes.2: Filtering a dry mixture does nothing, since both solids stay on the paper. Think about what must be done first so the salt can pass through.
notes.3: Evaporating a dry mixture does nothing, since there is no liquid. Think about what must be done first so the salt can pass through.

why.right: Dry salt is obtained this way because salt dissolves and passes through the filter paper while sand stays behind.
wrong: Dry salt is obtained this way because sand dissolves and passes through the filter paper while salt stays behind.
Dry salt is obtained this way because evaporation removes the sand as vapour before filtering.

questions.q: Ikan bilis is dried to keep it longer. Which technique is this?
questions.explain: Drying ikan bilis removes water from the fish by evaporation. Without water, bacteria cannot grow well, so the fish keeps longer.
questions.lo: Match everyday and industrial applications to separation techniques

notes.0: Chromatography separates coloured substances on paper. Think about what happens to the water in the fish as it dries.
notes.1: Nothing is passed through a filter when fish is dried. Think about what happens to the water in the fish as it dries.
notes.3: In distillation the vapour is collected, but drying fish does not collect the water. Think about what happens to the water in the fish.

why.right: Drying ikan bilis is evaporation because water leaves the fish as vapour and is not collected.
wrong: Drying ikan bilis is evaporation because the fish turns into vapour and only the water is left.
Drying ikan bilis is evaporation because the salt on the fish is collected as a pure liquid.

questions.q: Food testers check canned food for harmful colourings using
questions.explain: Chromatography separates the colourings in food into separate spots. Each spot can be compared with known harmful colourings.
questions.lo: Match everyday and industrial applications to separation techniques

notes.0: Evaporation would leave all the colourings mixed together. Think about a method that separates coloured substances.
notes.1: Food colourings are not magnetic. Think about a method that separates coloured substances.
notes.2: Dissolved colourings pass through filter paper together. Think about a method that separates coloured substances.

why.right: Chromatography can find harmful colourings because each colouring gives a spot that can be matched with a known one.
wrong: Chromatography can find harmful colourings because harmful substances always stay on the start line.
Chromatography can find harmful colourings because harmful colourings always boil off the paper first.

questions.q: Hairs and mucus in the nose trap dust particles. This is an example of
questions.explain: Hairs and mucus in the nose let air through but trap dust particles. This works like filter paper, so it is filtration.
questions.lo: Match everyday and industrial applications to separation techniques

notes.1: Nothing is heated or turned into vapour in the nose. Think about what happens to the dust as air passes through.
notes.2: Dust is not removed by magnetism. Think about what happens to the dust as air passes through.
notes.3: Nothing is boiled or condensed in the nose. Think about what happens to the dust as air passes through.

why.right: The nose acts as a filter because air passes through while larger dust particles are trapped.
wrong: The nose acts as a filter because the dust dissolves in mucus and turns into vapour.
The nose acts as a filter because the hairs attract dust particles like a magnet.

questions.q: Perfume is made by boiling petals and collecting the vapour. This is
questions.explain: The petals are boiled and the vapour is collected and cooled into a liquid. Boiling and condensing the vapour is distillation.
questions.lo: Match everyday and industrial applications to separation techniques

notes.0: Chromatography separates coloured substances on paper. Think about what is done to the vapour after it is collected.
notes.2: No filter is used to collect the vapour. Think about what is done to the vapour after it is collected.
notes.3: In evaporation the vapour escapes and is not collected. Here the vapour is collected. Think about which technique does this.

why.right: Making perfume this way is distillation because the vapour is collected and condensed into a liquid.
wrong: Making perfume this way is distillation because the petals are trapped on filter paper.
Making perfume this way is distillation because the vapour is allowed to escape into the air.

questions.q: Groundwater flows through sand and rocks in a siltation pond. This is
questions.explain: As groundwater flows through layers of sand and rocks, solid particles are trapped. This works like filter paper, so it is filtration.
questions.lo: Match everyday and industrial applications to separation techniques

notes.0: The water is not heated into vapour. Think about what the sand and rocks do to the solid particles in the water.
notes.2: Chromatography separates coloured substances on paper. Think about what the sand and rocks do to the solid particles in the water.
notes.3: Nothing is boiled or condensed. Think about what the sand and rocks do to the solid particles in the water.

why.right: Sand and rocks filter groundwater because water passes through the gaps while larger solid particles are trapped.
wrong: Sand and rocks filter groundwater because the solid particles dissolve into the sand and rocks as they pass.
Sand and rocks filter groundwater because they heat the water and make the solids evaporate.

questions.q: Which is one of Singapore's Four National Taps?
questions.explain: Singapore's Four National Taps are local catchment water, imported water, NEWater and desalinated water.
questions.lo: Name the Four National Taps and how tap water is treated

notes.1: Mineral water is bottled water from springs. It is not one of the Four National Taps. Think about the four sources that supply Singapore's water.
notes.2: Distilled water is made in laboratories and is not one of the Four National Taps. Think about the four sources that supply Singapore's water.
notes.3: Bottled water is a product people buy, not a national water source. Think about the four sources that supply Singapore's water.

questions.q: Where is rainwater from the local catchment stored?
questions.explain: Rainwater from the local catchment is collected through drains, canals and rivers, and stored in reservoirs.
questions.lo: Name the Four National Taps and how tap water is treated

notes.0: Desalination plants treat seawater, not rainwater. Think about where large amounts of collected rainwater are kept.
notes.1: NEWater plants treat used water. Think about where large amounts of collected rainwater are kept.
notes.3: Sewers carry used water away from homes. Think about where large amounts of collected rainwater are kept.

questions.q: At waterworks, water is chemically treated, filtered and then
questions.explain: At the waterworks, water is chemically treated, filtered and then disinfected. Disinfection kills harmful bacteria so the water is safe to drink.
questions.lo: Name the Four National Taps and how tap water is treated

notes.0: Water is not magnetised at the waterworks. Think about the step that makes the filtered water safe from germs.
notes.1: Distilling large amounts of water uses too much energy. Think about the step that makes the filtered water safe from germs.
notes.2: Evaporating the water would lose it. Think about the step that makes the filtered water safe from germs.

questions.q: NEWater is produced from
questions.explain: NEWater is made from used water that has been treated. It is purified further using microfiltration, reverse osmosis and ultraviolet disinfection.
questions.lo: Describe the steps used to produce NEWater

notes.1: Water made from seawater is desalinated water, a different National Tap. Think about water that has already been used.
notes.2: Imported water comes from Malaysia and is a different National Tap. Think about water that has already been used.
notes.3: Rainwater is collected as local catchment water, a different National Tap. Think about water that has already been used.

questions.q: What is the first purification step in a NEWater plant?
questions.explain: Microfiltration is the first step in a NEWater plant. It removes small solid particles and bacteria from the treated used water.
questions.lo: Describe the steps used to produce NEWater

notes.0: Distillation is not one of the NEWater steps. Think about the step that first filters out small particles.
notes.2: Ultraviolet disinfection is the final step, which kills any remaining germs. Think about the step that first filters out small particles.
notes.3: Reverse osmosis is the middle step. Think about the step that first filters out small particles.

questions.q: What is the last purification step in a NEWater plant?
questions.explain: Ultraviolet disinfection is the last step in a NEWater plant. It destroys any bacteria and viruses that are still left in the water.
questions.lo: Describe the steps used to produce NEWater

notes.0: Evaporation is not one of the NEWater steps. Think about the step that destroys any remaining germs.
notes.1: Microfiltration is the first step, which removes small particles. Think about the step that destroys any remaining germs.
notes.3: Reverse osmosis is the middle step. Think about the step that destroys any remaining germs.

questions.q: Which step comes right after microfiltration in a NEWater plant?
questions.explain: After microfiltration, the water goes through reverse osmosis. A membrane lets water particles through and holds back dissolved substances and remaining germs.
questions.lo: Describe the steps used to produce NEWater

notes.0: Evaporation is not one of the NEWater steps. Think about the step that pushes water through a membrane.
notes.1: Ultraviolet disinfection is the final step, not the second. Think about the step that pushes water through a membrane.
notes.2: Distillation is not one of the NEWater steps. Think about the step that pushes water through a membrane.

questions.q: A step destroys remaining bacteria and viruses with light. Which step is it?
questions.explain: Ultraviolet disinfection uses ultraviolet light to destroy any bacteria and viruses still left in the water.
questions.lo: Describe the steps used to produce NEWater

notes.0: Distillation uses boiling, not light. Think about which step uses a type of light that cannot be seen.
notes.1: Microfiltration uses a fine filter, not light. Think about which step uses a type of light that cannot be seen.
notes.2: Reverse osmosis uses a membrane, not light. Think about which step uses a type of light that cannot be seen.

questions.q: Obtaining drinking water from seawater is called
questions.explain: Desalination is the process of removing salt from seawater to obtain drinking water.
questions.lo: Describe desalination by distillation and reverse osmosis

notes.0: Reclamation is used for making new land or reusing water, not for treating seawater. Think about the word that means removing salt.
notes.2: Filtration cannot remove dissolved salt from seawater. Think about the term for removing salt from seawater.
notes.3: Chromatography separates coloured substances on paper. Think about the term for removing salt from seawater.

questions.q: Why is distillation not used for desalination in Singapore?
choices: heating seawater uses a lot of energy
questions.explain: Distillation needs seawater to be heated until it boils. This uses a lot of energy, which is costly for Singapore.
questions.lo: Describe desalination by distillation and reverse osmosis

notes.1: Distillation does remove salt, which stays behind when the water boils off. Think about what boiling large amounts of seawater needs.
notes.2: Distillation collects the water as distillate. Think about what boiling large amounts of seawater needs.
notes.3: Distillation produces pure water, because the salt stays behind. Think about what boiling large amounts of seawater needs.

why.right: Distillation is not used for desalination because boiling large amounts of seawater needs a lot of energy.
wrong: Distillation is not used for desalination because the salt boils off with the water and is collected.
Distillation is not used for desalination because the condenser lets salt pass into the distillate.

questions.q: In reverse osmosis, the membrane lets through
questions.explain: The membrane in reverse osmosis lets water particles through. Salt, other dissolved substances and germs are held back.
questions.lo: Describe desalination by distillation and reverse osmosis

notes.0: Bacteria are much larger than water particles and are held back by the membrane. Think about which particles are small enough to pass.
notes.1: Salt particles are held back by the membrane, which is how the salt is removed. Think about what passes through.
notes.3: If salt passed through, the water would still be salty. Think about which particles are small enough to pass.

why.right: The reverse osmosis membrane passes only water because its pores let water through but hold back salt particles.
wrong: The reverse osmosis membrane passes only water because it boils the water and leaves the salt behind.
The reverse osmosis membrane passes only water because the salt particles are attracted to a magnet in it.

questions.q: Which action reuses water?
choices: turning off the tap while brushing
watering plants with water used to wash vegetables
questions.explain: Reusing water means using the same water again for another job. Watering plants with water used to wash vegetables uses that water a second time.
questions.lo: Describe ways to conserve water and why water is precious

notes.0: Washing clothes on full load reduces water use, but it does not use the same water again. Look for water used a second time.
notes.1: Turning off the tap reduces water use, but it does not use the same water again. Look for water used a second time.
notes.2: Using the half-flush reduces water use, but it does not use the same water again. Look for water used a second time.

why.right: Watering plants with washing water is reuse because the same water is used again for a second job.
wrong: Watering plants with washing water is reuse because it uses less water than the first job did.
Watering plants with washing water is reuse because the water is cleaned at a NEWater plant first.

questions.q: Which action reduces water wastage?
choices: washing a few clothes at a time
washing the car with a running hose
washing the car with a pail of water
leaving the shower on while soaping
questions.explain: A pail holds a fixed amount of water, so less water is used. A running hose lets water flow out all the time, even when it is not needed.
questions.lo: Describe ways to conserve water and why water is precious

notes.0: Washing a few clothes at a time means more loads, which uses more water overall. Look for a way to use a fixed amount of water.
notes.1: A running hose lets water flow out even when it is not being used. Look for a way to use a fixed amount of water.
notes.3: Leaving the shower on while soaping lets water run down the drain unused. Look for a way to use a fixed amount of water.

why.right: Using a pail to wash a car reduces wastage because only a fixed amount of water is used.
wrong: Using a pail to wash a car reduces wastage because the water in a pail evaporates more slowly.
Using a pail to wash a car reduces wastage because pail water is cleaner than tap water.

questions.q: Why must Singapore conserve water?
questions.explain: Singapore has little land to collect and store rainwater, and it has no large natural water sources. Water is scarce, so it must be conserved.
questions.lo: Describe ways to conserve water and why water is precious

notes.1: Tap water in Singapore is treated and is safe to drink. Think about how much water Singapore can collect and store.
notes.2: Reservoirs do not store too much water, and the supply is limited. Think about how much water Singapore can collect and store.
notes.3: Water supply is not unlimited. Think about how much water Singapore can collect and store with its small land area.

why.right: Singapore must conserve water because it has limited land to collect and store rainwater.
wrong: Singapore must conserve water because treating tap water makes it unsafe to drink.
Singapore must conserve water because its reservoirs are too full to hold any more rain.
